data.title: D.C. appeals court sides with Pentagon on blacklist of Anthropic
data.description:
The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals sided with the Trump administration in its blacklisting of the artificial intelligence firm Anthropic, finding the Pentagon adequately backed up its decision to label the firm a national security risk.

The 2-1 ruling, issued Friday, rejected Anthropic’s challenge, finding the Department of Defense had “ample support” for its belief that the continued use of Anthropic’s Claude models by the agency or its contractors presented a national security risk.

“As Anthropic admits, the company encodes restrictions into Claude that prevent the model from performing tasks that Anthropic wishes to prevent,” Circuit Judge Gregory Kastas wrote for the majority.

“On more than one occasion, these restrictions have stopped Claude from performing tasks requested by government users,” Kastas continued.

Anthropic sued the Trump administration last month, challenging both the Pentagon’s designation — typically reserved for foreign adversaries — and President Trump’s directive for civilian agencies to stop using Anthropic’s products after negotiations fell apart over safety guardrails earlier this year.  

Anthropic requested its technology not be used in fully autonomous lethal weapons or for the mass surveillance of Americans, while the Pentagon insisted it be allowed to use Anthropic’s Claude for “all lawful uses.”

The court further determined Anthropic’s constitutional claims related to the First and Fifth Amendments were unfounded.

“Its due-process claim fails because the Department promptly notified the company of the exclusion and its supporting rationale, and then gave the company a fair opportunity to contest the exclusion,” Kastas wrote.

“And Anthropic’s First Amendment, claim fails because the Department excluded Anthropic from its supply chain based on the company’s refusal to assent to a contract term that the Department deemed essential, not based on the company’s support for greater governmental regulation of AI technology,” he continued.

Judge Neomi Rao joined Kastas in the majority, while Judge Karen LeCraft Henderson dissented, arguing the government interpreted the supply chain risk statute under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act, too broadly

Friday’s ruling breaks with a California federal judge’s decision last month finding the government violated the First Amendment when it issued the supply chain risk.

Rao agreed with Anthropic’s argument that the Trump administration retaliated against the Claude maker for its “constitutionally protected activity” and violated the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment.

The contradicting rulings could tee up a Supreme Court fight in the future. 

A spokesperson for Anthropic said the firm “respectfully disagrees” with the appeals court ruling.

“Another federal court has already held the government’s parallel designation unlawful,” they added. “We remain confident in our position and are considering all options, including further review.”

data.title: Supreme Court, overall liberal dissents, lets DHS overhaul immigration database for midterms
data.description:
The Supreme Court cleared the way on Friday for the Trump administration to implement its overhauled immigration database, which it says is aimed at combatting voter fraud, in time for November’s elections over the dissent of the liberal justices. 

The overhaul faced opposition from Democrats and some voting groups, and a judge had blocked it for violating federal privacy law. The Supreme Court’s emergency ruling lifts that block, finding the challengers’ claims are likely to fail. 

The majority wrote that “the Federal Government has an obligation to respond to requests from state and local election officials seeking to verify the citizenship of voters.” 

“The order below prevents the Federal Government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task,” the court wrote. 

DHS’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) is used to determine eligibility for certain federal programs.

DHS made significant updates after President Trump directed the agency to ensure election officials had appropriate access to verify their voters’ citizenship. The changes connect SAVE to Social Security records and allow bulk queries, among other updates. 

The three liberal justices publicly dissented, led by Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson. 

“In my view, however, the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take,” Jackson wrote, joined by Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan. 

It is not a final ruling, but the justices’ order means the overhaul can proceed for the midterms as the litigation continues. The case now returns to the lower courts. 

The dispute is among election-related emergency litigation that has swarmed the Supreme Court in the lead-up to the midterms. 

Trump’s win comes just days after the court ruled against him on his mail-in voting plan. And days earlier, the court ruled against Missouri Republicans by lifting a judge’s directive to proceed with their new congressional map. That case has now returned to the justices once again. 

Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the Supreme Court that the SAVE overhaul is needed to protect election integrity. 

“DHS’s SAVE system was not up to the job because it lacked comprehensive data about natural-born citizens, permitted searches only one record at a time, and required the user to supply a person’s alien registration number (or other DHS number)—which States often do not know,” Sauer explained. 

U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan, an appointee of former President Biden, blocked it in June. She found the changes violated the Social Security Act and a federal law that regulates how the government can disclose individuals’ personal data. 

The Trump administration brought her ruling to the Supreme Court after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit declined to lift her order in a 2-1 vote. 

Voting groups called the overhaul “unprecedented” in their filings with the Supreme Court and urged the justices to not get involved. 

“Congress has not authorized the federal government to create a master database of U.S. citizens. Nor does the government possess any dataset capable of providing accurate, real-time verification of individuals’ U.S. citizenship status,” the League of Women Voters wrote in its response.

data.title: Banning H-1B teachers is a recipe for disaster
data.description:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) wants public schools in his state to employ “exactly zero” employees on H-1B visas.

His campaign-trail proposal would completely bar schools from employing anyone on the specialized work permit, impacting new hires and current teachers. If passed, this would be a stark reversal for the state that, in 2025, received more K-12 education H-1B visa approvals than any other.

Abbott’s rationale prioritizes protection against vague threats of “foreign influence” over the mundane but tangible consequences of thousands of students losing access to qualified teachers. H-1B reliant Dallas Independent School District bluntly described the implications: If these teachers go, it will need more Texans in the pipeline.

But the Texas pipeline of qualified teachers is running dry. We have each spent years studying teachers in America’s most challenged schools and the difficult decisions made in response to teacher shortages. Our findings demonstrate how educationally reckless the governor’s proposal is.

Our research, looking at three decades of math and science teacher qualifications, surfaced a significant finding: STEM teacher qualifications in the highest-need settings have been stable, even modestly improving. This is occurring despite the teaching profession being at a 50-year low, including coinciding enrollment drops in teacher preparation programs and relative declines in teachers’ pay.    

How is it, then, that STEM teacher quality has been sustained, even improved? High-need schools got creative.  

Recruiting foreign-trained teachers emerged as a critical stopgap. Foreign teachers’ share of the science, technology, engineering and mathematics workforce in high-need schools grew from 1 percent in 1993 to more than 6 percent by 2020. They are concentrated where teacher shortages are worst: math, science, special education and foreign languages in high-poverty urban and rural schools.   

In addition, foreign-trained teachers are, on average, more qualified than their U.S.-trained counterparts. In our study, 79 percent held a STEM degree, compared to 68 percent of their peers. Their graduate training was higher, too. Our in-depth examination of migrant teachers shows that these are not low-quality hires, but top-tier educators recruited to schools that domestic applicants avoid.   

If the ban passes, the consequences will be immediate and predictable, including more out-of-field teaching and long-term substitutes. But the most common teacher shortage stopgap in Texas is employing instructional staff without any formal training at all. In the 2023-24 school year, more than half of new Texas teachers entered without any certification, and research shows their students learn less. The ban would accelerate a substitution already underway, trading qualified teachers for unprepared alternatives.  

Let’s consider the “foreign influence” threat worrying Abbott. He cited a Qatari-supported Arabic language program and Chinese-backed Mandarin instruction. These programs can and should be debated, but they implicate very few Texas teachers. By contrast, he expressed no concern about the many certified Filipino or Mexican teachers, yet they would be swept up in far greater numbers.   

Furthermore, banning H-1Bs will not shrink the demand for international teachers — it funnels employers toward J-1 visas, designed for cultural exchange, not labor shortages. That’s not a fix; it’s a swap for a more short-term, unstable working credential. What’s more, it fails to curtail the “foreign influence” motivating Abbott’s proposal while mechanically increasing teacher turnover.  

U.S. schools should not rely indefinitely on international teacher recruitment. We have written about the risks of that dependency: the precarity of visa-tied teachers, the moral questions raised by drawing top talent from developing countries, and the vulnerability created when a pandemic, diplomatic disruption or $100,000 visa fee can suddenly cut off the supply.   

The right response, though, is to invest in a stronger domestic pipeline. That means expanding programs like the National Science Foundation’s Robert Noyce Teacher Scholarship Program, which our research shows have improved STEM teacher qualifications and supply. UTeach, a Texas-born program now operating in more than a dozen states, has likewise increased the STEM teacher pipeline. Policymakers should also increase teacher pay and differentiate in subjects and schools experiencing shortages. Finally, they should remediate the working conditions that make schools difficult to staff in the first place.   

Texas’s teacher pipeline has grown thinner and less prepared on Abbott’s watch. The children in the state’s high-need schools have been protected, in part, by the qualified international teachers he now proposes to expel. 

Michael Hansen is a senior fellow in the Brown Center on Education Policy at the Brookings Institution. Lora Bartlett is the chairwoman of the education department at the University of California, Santa Cruz, and co-author of “Going the Distance: The Teaching Profession in a Post-COVID World.”

data.title: Behind on bills? Residents of these states have seen debt balloon
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – People who live in some of the country’s most affordable states have seen their debt double over the past 10 years, a new data analysis shows.

Residents of Idaho and Utah have an average debt that is 100% higher than it was a decade ago, according to a study MoneyLion shared with Nexstar.

The analysis takes into account both “good debt” – like a mortgage – and “bad debt” – like credit card balances. School and car loans were also factored in.

Idaho residents, on average, saw major increases in auto, mortgage and credit card debt between 2015 and 2025. The increase in student loans wasn’t as dramatic, only about 26%.

Credit card debt, which carries some of the highest interest rates, went up the most in Nevada. The state saw its collective credit card debt jump from $6 billion in 2015 to more than $14 billion in 2025.

A home loan, meanwhile, isn’t considered quite as toxic as some other types of debt because the asset it’s used to purchase is expected to appreciate over time. Mortgage debt went up the most in Idaho, Utah and Texas. All three states have been seen as desirable places to move since the pandemic with growing populations.

There’s bad news for borrowers: The Federal Reserve just raised the cost of borrowing money.

The Fed increased its benchmark interest rate last week by a quarter-point, the first rate hike since the summer of 2023. The increase boosts the Fed’s target rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%.

Anyone borrowing money to make a sizable purchase, such as a home, car or large appliance, will likely take a hit eventually. The new rate will also increase monthly payments and costs for any consumer who is already paying interest on credit card debt.

For now, U.S. household debt payments are relatively low overall as a percentage of after-tax income. So even if borrowing rates rise, many households might not feel a heavier debt burden immediately.

On the bright side, if you’ve been socking money away, you’ll probably earn a bit more interest on your savings.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

data.title: Beware of billionaires gifting Trojan Horses to steal your election data
data.description:
It’s fitting that millions of Americans spent this summer revisiting “The Odyssey” and getting reacquainted with the ancient world’s most infamous trick: the Trojan Horse. Perhaps it means we are all a bit more prepared to be skeptical of certain gifts.

Because earlier this month, Americans got a look inside Elon Musk’s own Trojan Horse. =

It’s called VoteSafe.org. On the surface, the site — operated by Musk’s America PAC — looks like a public resource designed to help Americans register to vote, check their registration or find their polling place. Underneath, it is a sophisticated political data operation.

VoteSafe.org is not new. Musk launched the site in 2024. What is new is what America PAC can do with the data it collects.

American PAC has reportedly rewritten the site’s privacy policy on Aug. 29, allowing it to share personal information such as name, age, address, email, phone number and IP address with advertisers, political organizations and other unaffiliated third parties. It can also sell “inferences” it makes from the information it collects from users, including “psychological trends, predispositions, behavior, attitudes, intelligence, abilities, and aptitude.”

That data is valuable. I know because I run Vote.org, the largest nonpartisan voter registration and get-out-the-vote technology platform in the country.

That’s exactly why we protect it. We don’t use voters’ information to support or oppose candidates. We don’t use data to manipulate your opinion or behavior. And we most certainly don’t sell voters’ data to the highest bidder.  

VoteSafe.org does not exist in isolation. It is part of a broader and troubling pattern in which politically connected technology operations are moving into civic spaces that depend on public trust.

This summer, the Guardian reported  that the National Design Studio — “an opaque White House office” led by Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia and staffed in part by veterans of Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency operation — had built a copy of the website Vote.gov on White House-controlled infrastructure. The actual Vote.gov site is supposed to be run by an independent, bipartisan commission — the Election Assistance Commission.

The proposed copycat site would have required voters to verify their identities and check their citizenship against a Department of Homeland Security database. It would also have allowed White House officials to access user data.

To be clear, that copycat site is not the Vote.gov Americans use today. According to the Election Assistance Commission, the White House effort was paused and the current public site remains on infrastructure controlled by the commission with no connection to White House systems. But given the opacity surrounding the whole thing, that official assurance does not resolve every question about where data may flow on the backend.

This episode should concern anyone who cares about trustworthy elections. Congress placed federal election assistance in the hands of an independent, bipartisan commission — not the White House — for a reason. Moving voter registration services onto infrastructure controlled by any sitting president would blur an important line between neutral election administration and partisan political power. It would also raise serious questions about what information is collected, who can access it, and how it might be used. 

VoteSafe.org and the National Design Studio are both examples of political operations trying to assert control over machinery voters depend on to participate in our democracy — and that’s incredibly dangerous. 

This is exactly why the work of organizations like ours that provide independent, nonpartisan resources with accurate and credible information to voters with no ulterior motives matters so much right now. Voters shouldn’t have to trade their personal information just to find out how to register or where to vote. And they shouldn’t have to wonder whether the voting website in front of them is a neutral public service or a political operation angling for their data.  

They should be able to trust that the site in front of them is what it claims to be, and not a Trojan Horse. 

Andrea Hailey is CEO of Vote.org.

data.title: Massie: Trump 'comeuppance' will happen on Election Day
data.description:
GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.), who lost his primary to an opponent backed by President Trump, predicted a reckoning for the president and the GOP in the midterm elections.

“I think his comeuppance will happen on Election Day, and the day after I think there’s going to be a reckoning,” the Republican lawmaker said during an interview Thursday with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins on “The Source.”

Massie, who was defeated in the GOP primary by Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein, has been an outspoken critic of the president and his administration’s policies. 

The Republican lawmaker has crossed party lines to support several Iran war powers resolutions and led a bipartisan push in the House for the release of the Justice Department’s files related to its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. 

Collins asked the Kentucky Republican on Thursday specifically about the decision of several Republicans running for reelection this cycle to criticize tactics used by federal officers in the Trump administration’s nationwide immigration enforcement operations. 

“I was the Republican who was speaking out for so long, and they were all whatever Trump wants, they were all for it in their primaries,” Massie said. “They’re about to take a shellacking here in the general election, so they’re running from him on this and other issues, like the war.”

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas), who is engaged in a tight battle in Kansas to retain his seat this November, said Thursday he expressed concerns to the Department of Homeland Security about the immigration operations and urged they be carried out in a “responsible and secure manner.”

Massie also criticized the president’s decision to host Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House for a lavish state dinner on Thursday evening, saying it sends a “mixed message.”

“He will invite a communist to the White House, but I can’t even go there for the Christmas party,” the Republican said. “His retribution tour on Republicans, I think, stands in stark contrast to the way he’s treating the communist leader of China and also the mayor of New York.

“But you know, that’s just who he is,” Massie added. “He’s not an ideologue. He doesn’t have a true north, or honestly any kind of beliefs.”

data.title: Ed Sheeran loses nearly half a million Instagram followers amid Macklemore drama
data.description:
(NewsNation) — Ed Sheeran has lost nearly half a million followers on social media after controversy over his recent tour and his decision to drop opening act Macklemore over statements supporting Palestine.

Macklemore said on Instagram that his ouster was at the behest of Robert Kraft, owner of Gillette Stadium. The “Thrift Shop” singer said Kraft organized a group of stadium owners in a boycott, telling Sheeran that he would not be allowed to perform if he did not drop the rapper from the set.

Sheeran’s other opening acts also departed the tour in solidarity with Macklemore, who emphasized that the real victims in the scenario are not famous music artists but the Palestinian people.

Sheeran had avoided politics during his career but became caught in the middle after Macklemore’s statements.

An emotional Sheeran apologized to fans at one show and admitted that the debate has cost him close, personal relationships.

The incident has also sparked larger questions about free speech, with some public figures maintaining that politics and art should be kept separate and others saying it is part of a larger conversation about whether those with powerful interests should be able to control what artists can say.

Macklemore also recently announced he would be launching his own series of concerts to benefit Palestinian aid organizations.

data.title: Washington must rejoin the Saudi war against the Houthis
data.description:
The Houthis have been in an intermittent war with Saudi Arabia for a dozen years, but their resentment of Saudi Arabia stretches back nearly a century.

In the 1920s, King Abdul Aziz of Saudi Arabia seized the Asir province that historically had been under Zaidi Muslim control. When the rulers of Yemen tried to reclaim the territory, they were defeated by the Saudis in 1934. The Houthis, a mountain people, are Zaidis, the Saudis are Wahhabi Sunnis. The Houthis are committed to restoring Zaidi rule, which had ended in 1962, and continue to resent the loss of Asir. 

In 2004, the Houthis revolted against the north Yemeni government of Ali Saleh when Saleh sought to arrest their leader, Hussein Badereddin al-Houthi. Al-Houthi died the same year, but the rebellion did not die with him. As the war dragged on, the Saudis intervened on behalf of Saleh’s government.

Ten years after their initial uprising, the Houthis captured Sana’a, the ancient north Yemeni capital. In response, the Saudis, with American intelligence and logistical support, tried but failed to drive back the Houthis. Instead, with Iranian assistance, including arms and trainers, the Houthis continued to expand their control over north Yemeni territory.

After several years of peace, the Houthis intervened on behalf of Hamas in its war with Israel. In 2024 they fired missiles at Israel, prompting Israeli attacks on their formations. They also attacked Israeli-linked shipping in the Red Sea, expanded those attacks to ships from other countries, and fired missiles and drones on American and British naval units that were defending vessels transiting the Red and Arabian seas.

The attacks continued when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in 2025, and after holding their fire after renewed American operations against Iran in February, the Houthis, with Iranian encouragement, seized key islands in the Bab el Mandeb strait and closed it to Saudi shipping. They also attacked Saudi military and civilian targets, including targeting drones and missiles on Mecca and Riyadh.

The Saudis are receiving support from Pakistan, their Mecca Treaty allies, which has deployed 8,000 troops and air defense systems, and has sent a squadron of Chinese-built J-17 fighter aircraft to the King Abdul Aziz air base. The 600 miles from the base to the Houthi strongholds constitutes the outer limits of the fighters’ combat radius, however. It would be difficult to conduct more than one attack before having to return to base.

In any event, the Pakistanis have thus far not launched any attacks on the Houthis, and their forces are likely to remain in a defensive posture. 

Riyadh’s other Mecca Treaty allies, the Turks, have offered to assist the Saudis, but thus far have not committed forces to defend them or attack the Houthis — no doubt because Ankara’s forces continue to operate in Syria and Iraq.

Thanks to Houthi attacks on both Red Sea shipping and Saudi oil pipelines, together with its chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz, Iran has been able to throttle Saudi oil exports. The kingdom is facing the prospect of economic contraction, while finding itself unable to defeat the Houthis, especially as it continues to suffer from Iranian missile attacks. 

Riyadh has turned to America for assistance, but thus far the Saudis have been rebuffed. Washington is committed to its operations against Iran and faces an increasing munitions shortfall that would seriously worsen if it again joined the fight against the Houthis, who have threatened to retaliate.

Leaving the Saudis to their own devices will simply encourage Riyadh to reevaluate its relationship with the U.S., however. Its defense strategy has been predicated on America’s rushing to its defense in the event of Iranian attack, yet until now American forces have been unable to prevent Iranian missiles and drones from inflicting extensive damage on Saudi military and civilian targets.

No doubt China, which long has had an excellent economic relationship with the Saudis and in the past has sold them weapons, would act quickly to fill any vacuum that Washington leaves. Should the Saudis turn toward China and away from the U.S., several of the smaller Gulf states — notably Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar, which have also suffered from Iranian attacks — would likely follow suit. With Oman continuing to discuss a joint arrangement with Iran to manage the strait of Hormuz, only the United Arab Emirates might stand with America to confront the Iranians. 

Ceding the region to China surely is not a prospect Washington should relish, even if it wishes to lower its Middle Eastern profile. For that reason, it would behoove the Trump administration to reconsider its rejection of Saudi entreaties, and, despite the materiel shortages it surely confronts, come to the aid of its longstanding Middle Eastern ally. 

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

data.title: Chinese media scuffle with US journalists, Secret Service during Xi visit
data.description:
Members of the Chinese press corps traveling with President Xi Jinping scuffled with U.S. journalists and Secret Service personnel at the White House on Thursday as reporters scrambled to cover the Chinese leader’s state visit.

Videos posted online showed several confrontations throughout the day, including Chinese journalists arguing with White House staff and Secret Service agents over where they could stand during Xi’s arrival ceremony and military review in the Rose Garden.

One video showed journalists packed together as they competed for space ahead of Xi’s arrival. An American journalist could be heard saying, “You’re stepping on my feet.”

Another dispute broke out on the South Law over the positioning of U.S. outlets and Chinese state media.

Washington Examiner White House correspondent Christian Datoc said Secret Service and White House officials threatened to remove a Chinese official who was interfering with official White House camera positions.

Video from the scene showed agents attempting to move members of the Chinese press as voices were raised.

Tensions continued inside the White House, where a Chinese photographer reportedly shoved a female American reporter in a packed briefing room as journalists rushed to cover President Trump and Xi’s meeting in the Oval Office.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth also reportedly reacted to a disruption created by the Chinese press corps in the Grand Foyer of the White House, according to Daily Wire White House correspondent Mary Margaret Olohan, who described the visiting press corps as “incredibly loud and aggressive.”

Trump reportedly joked that China had the friendliest press corps.

The confrontations unfolded during a chaotic day for the White House press corps.

Journalists from major television networks ABC, CBS News, NBC News and Fox News were present at the White House, but continued withholding their participation in the television pool until they received confirmation that CNN, MS Now and Politico had regained access to the complex.

The three outlets, barred from the White House by Trump last week, were allowed back in around midday Thursday after a federal judge ordered the White House to restore their access, following a court hearing on Wednesday.

Still, some CNN and MS NOW reporters were blocked from covering the state dinner for Xi on Thursday evening.

data.title: Trump mourns death of man shot at Butler rally: 'Tremendous loss'
data.description:
President Trump mourned the loss of Jim Copenhaver, the man who was shot and injured during the attempted assassination on Trump’s life in Butler, Pa., in 2024.

Copenhaver died earlier this week. He was 76. He was one of the two attendees who were shot at the rally where a bullet grazed Trump’s ear. Copenhaver was struck by two bullets in his arm and abdomen, leaving him with nerve damage.

“God bless American Patriot and Warrior, James Copenhaver, and his incredible family. May he rest in peace!!!” Trump wrote on Truth Social Friday. 

He called Copenhaver a “true American patriot” in a post Thursday, saying his death is a “tremendous loss.”

“More than two years ago in Butler, Pennsylvania, a crazed gunman attempted to stifle our America First Movement. Instead, Jim and so many other wonderful Patriots who love our Country, stood united in defense of our shared values of Freedom, Liberty, and Justice,” Trump wrote. 

“After being wounded while protecting his family, Jim showed tremendous bravery, courageously continuing to FIGHT, FIGHT, FIGHT, and maintaining a positive spirit despite unimaginable hardships,” he continued. “His indelible legacy of love and devotion will forever endure. Our hearts and prayers are with the Copenhaver family, especially his incredible wife Marianne. God bless you all!”

His death was first announced by the House Republican Conference on Thursday. 

“We are deeply saddened by the passing of Jim Copenhaver, who was gravely wounded in the horrific shooting in Butler, Pennsylvania,” the conference posted on social media. 

Several Republican lawmakers also responded to the news of Copenhaver’s death. 

“My prayers are with the family members of Jim Copenhaver, as they grieve his loss,” Arizona Rep. Andy Biggs (R) wrote in a post. “His passing should serve as continued motivation to provide sufficient answers and closure for the investigation into the attempted assassination of President Trump in Butler, where two innocent lives have now been lost.”
